source_text: Prior ergo sententia tua nihil obscuritate promovebit; secunda vero, qua repetis, quoniam liberum quidem confiteris arbitrium, non tamen ut quisquam homo liber ad agendum bonum credatur, viscera tua tota nudavit.
pass_a_gloss: Your prior sentence therefore will promote nothing by obscurity; but the second, by which you repeat that you indeed confess free choice, yet not that any human be believed free for doing good, has bared all your viscera.

lemmas.lexica: LS bonum; Blaise good-of-nature vs good-of-will
LS liber=free; also children; context decides

pass_b_english: Your first statement, then, will gain nothing through its obscurity. Your second, in which you repeat that you acknowledge free will, yet do not believe any human being free to do good, has laid your whole inner self bare.

choices.why: Keep Julian's good-of-nature vs good-of-will contrast; do not baptize as 'grace'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
